source_text:
καὶ

τοιοῦτόν ἐστιν ὅ φησιν ὁ σωτήρ· ὥσπερ γὰρ ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις τοῦ Νῶε ἦσαν
γαμοῦντες καὶ γαμισκόμενοι, καὶ ἐξάπινα ἦλθεν ὁ κατακλυσμὸς καὶ ἔλαβε πάντας,
οὕτως ἔσται ἡ παρουσία τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου. οὐκοῦν, φησίν, ζῶντες
καταλαμβάνονταί τινες. Ἐν κελεύσματι καὶ ἐν φωνῇ ἀρχαγγέλου, καὶ οἱ νεκροὶ ἐν
Χριστῷ ἀναστήσονται. τοῦτο αὐτὸς ὁ κύριος λέγει ἐν τῷ Εὐαγγελίῳ· μέσης δὲ οὔσης
νυκτός, φησί, φωνὴ ἐγένετο· ὁ νυμφίος ἔρχεται. ὅτι δὲ ζῶντες καταλαμβάνονται, οἳ
καὶ ἀναλαμβάνονται μετὰ τῶν κοιμηθέντων, ὁ κύριος δηλοῖ ἐν τῷ Εὐαγγελίῳ
λέγων· δύο ἔσονται ἐν κλίνῃ· ὁ εἷς παραληφθήσεται, καὶ ὁ εἷς ἀφεθήσεται. καὶ δύο
ἔσονται ἀλήθουσαι· ἡ μία παραληφθήσεται, καὶ ἡ μία ἀφεθήσεται. καὶ ὁ κύριός τε
καὶ ὁ Παῦλος αἰνίττονται ὅτι νυκτὸς ἔσται ἡ παρουσία. 1 Thess 5,4®5 Ἡμέραν κυρίου
τὴν παρουσίαν αὐτοῦ λέγει. κλέπτῃ δὲ παρείκασεν αὐτήν, ὅτι λανθάνουσα καὶ παρὰ
προσδοκίαν ἔρχεται. ἐν νυκτὶ δέ, ὅτι ἡ ἡμέρα ἐπιστᾶσα τὰ ἐν νυκτὶ φαῦλα ἀπελέγχει.
331 1 Thess 5,6®8 Ἀλλ' ἡ νύμφη καὶ τῷ τῶν ἀρετῶν κόσμῳ κοσμουμένη ψυχὴ τὸν
τῆς ἡμέρας ὕπνον καθεύδουσα τὸν ἄμοιρον νυκτὸς τὸν τῇ ἐγρηγόρσει
συνεζευγμένον, καὶ μάλα εἰκότως ἔλεγεν· ἐγὼ καθεύδω, καὶ ἡ καρδία μου γρηγορεῖ.
thought_title: The Lord's coming at night overtakes the living
orientation: Severianus is explaining 1 Thessalonians 4:16-17 and 5:4-8, showing from the Gospels that the Lord's coming will be at night and will overtake some who are still alive.
pass_a_gloss: And such is what the Savior says: For just as in the days of Noah they were marrying and being given in marriage, and suddenly the flood came and took everyone, so will be the coming of the son of man. Therefore, he says, some are overtaken while living. With a shout of command and with the voice of an archangel, and the dead in Christ will rise. This the Lord himself says in the Gospel: and while it was midnight, he says, a voice came: the bridegroom is coming. And that the living are overtaken, who also are taken up together with those who have fallen asleep, the Lord makes clear in the Gospel saying: two will be in one bed; the one will be taken, and the one will be left. And two will be grinding; the one will be taken, and the one will be left. And both the Lord and Paul hint that the coming will be at night. Day of the Lord he calls his coming. And he has likened it to a thief, because it comes unnoticed and contrary to expectation. And at night, because the day when it has arrived exposes the evil things done at night. But the bride, the soul adorned also with the ornament of virtues, sleeping the sleep of the day that has no share in night, the sleep joined to wakefulness, very reasonably said: I sleep, and my heart is awake.

choices.why: Passive form of γαμίσκομαι, distinct from the active γαμοῦντες; preserves the passive force of the source.
κέλευσμα is a word of command or signal, often a shout; renders the military or authoritative force of the term.
The verb means to be seized or caught up with; 'overtaken' preserves the sense of being caught while still living.
The participle of ἀλήθω means grinding grain; feminine plural agrees with the two women in the Gospel saying.
The verb means to speak in riddles or hint at something indirectly; preserves the indirectness of the source.
The compound means to refute or expose thoroughly; 'exposes' captures the revealing force of the day against night deeds.

pass_b_english: And this is what the Savior says: “For as in the days of Noah they were marrying and being given in marriage, and suddenly the flood came and took them all, so will be the coming of the Son of Man” (Matthew 24:38-39). So, he says, some are overtaken while still living. “With a shout of command and with the voice of an archangel, and the dead in Christ will rise” (1 Thessalonians 4:16). The Lord himself says this in the Gospel: “At midnight,” he says, “there was a cry: The bridegroom is coming” (Matthew 25:6). And that some are overtaken while living—those who are taken up together with those who have fallen asleep—the Lord makes clear in the Gospel when he says: “Two will be in one bed; one will be taken and one will be left. Two will be grinding; one will be taken and one will be left” (Luke 17:34-35). Both the Lord and Paul hint that the coming will be at night.

He calls his coming the day of the Lord. He has likened it to a thief because it comes unnoticed and unexpectedly. And he says it is at night because the day, when it arrives, exposes the evil deeds done at night.

But the bride—the soul adorned with the adornment of virtues—sleeping the sleep of the day, the sleep that has no share in night, the sleep yoked to wakefulness, said with good reason: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song of Songs 5:2).

last_rejected.quote: He calls his coming the day of the Lord. He has likened it to a thief because it comes unnoticed and unexpectedly. And he says it is at night because the day, when it arrives, exposes the evil deeds done at night.
last_rejected.source_quote: Ἡμέραν κυρίου τὴν παρουσίαν αὐτοῦ λέγει. κλέπτῃ δὲ παρείκασεν αὐτήν, ὅτι λανθάνουσα καὶ παρὰ προσδοκίαν ἔρχεται. ἐν νυκτὶ δέ, ὅτι ἡ ἡμέρα ἐπιστᾶσα τὰ ἐν νυκτὶ φαῦλα ἀπελέγχει.
last_rejected.why: The English 'He calls... He has likened... he says' hides that this is Severianus commenting on Paul (from 'φησίν' earlier and the lemma citation 1 Thess 5:4-5). The subject shifts to Paul/Severianus exposition but English uses ambiguous 'He'.
last_rejected.fix: Paul calls his coming the day of the Lord. He has likened it...
last_rejected.ruling: Greek subject ambiguous; English 'He' acceptable, not a clear misattribution

last_rejected.quote: the sleep that has no share in night
last_rejected.why: English adds 'sleep' before 'that has no share in night' but Greek has τὸν ἄμοιρον νυκτός as apposition to τὸν τῆς ἡμέρας ὕπνον. The English 'the sleep that has no share in night' is accurate. No error.
last_rejected.ruling: Translation matches meaning of τὸν ἄμοιρον νυκτός

last_rejected.quote: Both the Lord and Paul hint that the coming will be at night.
last_rejected.source_quote: καὶ ὁ κύριός τε καὶ ὁ Παῦλος αἰνίττονται ὅτι νυκτὸς ἔσται ἡ παρουσία.
last_rejected.why: Wait, checking if anything omitted before this... The Greek has '1 Thess 5,4®5' citation marker before Ἡμέραν κυρίου. English includes this content but check: does English include '1 Thess 5:4-5'? Looking: English has 'He calls his coming the day of the Lord.' The citation marker is omitted in English, but the content is present. The lemma citation is editorial marking, not author text. Not an omission error.
last_rejected.ruling: Citation marker omitted is editorial, not text

last_rejected.quote: those who are taken up together with those who have fallen asleep
last_rejected.source_quote: οἳ καὶ ἀναλαμβάνονται μετὰ τῶν κοιμηθέντων
last_rejected.why: English 'taken up' for ἀναλαμβάνονται is slightly different from 'taken' παραληφθήσεται earlier. But ἀναλαμβάνομαι can mean 'taken up' in sense of received/assumed. In context of eschatology, 'taken up' works. However, the key issue: English says 'those who are taken up together with those who have fallen asleep' but Greek οἳ καὶ ἀναλαμβάνονται μετὰ τῶν κοιμηθέντων means 'who are also taken up with those who have fallen asleep' — the 'also/and' (καὶ) is slightly misplaced in English. 'those who are taken up together with' = μετὰ. Actually this is fine. But wait: the Greek says οἳ καὶ ἀναλαμβάνονται — 'who also are taken up' not 'who are taken up together with'. The καὶ goes with ἀναλαμβάνονται, not μετά. English 'those who are taken up together with' makes 'together with' seem like the only point, but 'also' is important: they are overtaken while living, AND they are taken up with the dead. English 'together with' captures μετά but loses the 'also' (καὶ). Is this omission? The sense is slightly reduced but not lost: 'taken up together with' implies joint action. Not clearly wrong.
last_rejected.fix: those who are also taken up with those who have fallen asleep
last_rejected.ruling: English conveys Greek meaning; loss of καὶ minor, not major
